Rakali (Hydromys chrysogaster) exhibit a set of developmental milestones that are tightly linked to their semi-aquatic lifestyle and relatively slow life-history pace for an Australian murid rodent. Neonates emerge after a gestation period lasting 34 days [tg = 34 days] when the mother maintains a core body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], a thermal regime that supports efficient embryogenesis. The newborn pups weigh approximately 31.4 grams [Wwb = approximately 31.4 grams], a modest mass reflecting the altricial state typical of native rodents, though the young develop rapidly under intensive maternal care. Field studies tracking known individuals in coastal waterways of New South Wales indicate that the single litter typically numbers 3.29 pups [N_R_i = 3.29 pups], a relatively small litter size compared to many small murids, consistent with an energy allocation strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity in a competitive aquatic niche. The daily reproductive rate derived from this modest litter combined with a breeding frequency of 2.6 litters per year [F_R_i = 2.6 litters per year] at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C] suggests a measured pace of population turnover, likely constrained by the energetic demands of foraging in cold water.

The period of neonatal dependency culminates in weaning, a critical transition to nutritional independence that occurs 29 days after birth [tx = 29 days after birth] at the typical maternal body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. At this developmental juncture, the weaned juveniles leave the den weighing approximately 150 grams [Wwx = approximately 150 grams], having more than quadrupled their birth mass through a diet of mother's milk supplemented by small aquatic prey items masticated by the female. This weaning weight represents a substantial investment by the mother, as the young must achieve sufficient body size to capture their own prey—primarily freshwater crayfish and small fish—immediately following nutritional emancipation. Comparative data from other hydromyine rodents suggest that this 29-day suckling phase (29 days after birth) [tx = 29 days after birth] is intermediate in duration, reflecting a balance between the benefits of extended maternal provisioning and the need for the mother to recycle energy into subsequent reproductive efforts at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. The attainment of this weaning mass is a reliable indicator of successful transition to the juvenile life stage, after which growth trajectories become increasingly shaped by individual foraging success and territory quality.

Juveniles that survive the post-weaning period enter a prolonged sub-adult phase characterized by sustained somatic growth and the gradual development of the dense, waterproof pelage essential for efficient aquatic foraging. Growth curves constructed from mark-recapture data indicate that individuals attain the wet weight at puberty of 433 grams [Wwp = 433 grams] after a period of sustained feeding. Interestingly, the timing of sexual maturation is sexually dimorphic in this species, a common pattern among mammals with polygynous or promiscuous mating systems. Females typically first exhibit signs of reproductive maturity at a younger chronological age, reaching puberty 124 days since birth [tp = 124 days since birth] under the stable thermal conditions of a 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C] core body temperature. Males, in contrast, require a longer developmental period to achieve physiological readiness for reproduction, with the onset of gonadal activity recorded at 135 days since birth [tp = 135 days since birth] at the same temperature at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C].

Adult Rakali are among the largest of the Australian native rodents, with a robust, streamlined body adapted for an amphibious existence. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults is approximately 850 grams [Wwi = approximately 850 grams], a size that places them at the upper end of the body mass range for Australian murids and facilitates dominance in their freshwater habitats. This substantial adult body mass is supported by a diet rich in protein from aquatic invertebrates and vertebrates, and the energetic surplus allows for the maintenance of a thick, insulating fur coat that is critical for thermoregulation during dives in cool water. Long-term field studies conducted in the Murray-Darling basin and coastal lagoons of Victoria have documented a maximum lifespan in the wild of 7.3 years [am = 7.3 years] at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], a remarkably extended longevity for a rodent of this body size. This lifespan, equivalent to over 2,600 days of active life, is considerably greater than that of most small native rodents, which rarely exceed two years, and is more typical of larger, slower-reproducing mammals. The interplay between a large body size and a long lifespan aligns with predictions from life-history theory that reduced extrinsic mortality in aquatic predators selects for delayed senescence.

The ecological and physiological interplay between body size, reproductive output, and longevity underscores the unique position of Hydromys chrysogaster within the Australian mammal community. The substantial investment in each offspring, evidenced by the transition from a 31.4-gram neonate (31.4 grams) [Wwb = 31.4 grams] to a 150-gram weanling (150 grams) [Wwx = 150 grams] in just 29 days after birth [tx = 29 days after birth], is energetically feasible only because the species occupies a productive, protein-rich ecological niche at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. The extended growth to an adult mass of 850 grams [Wwi = 850 grams] and the delayed attainment of the 433-gram pubertal mass (433 grams) [Wwp = 433 grams]—occurring at 124 days since birth [tp = 124 days since birth] in females and 135 days since birth [tp = 135 days since birth] in males—demonstrate a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic durability over rapid generational turnover at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C] at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. This strategy is further underscored by the maximum longevity of 7.3 years [am = 7.3 years], which provides an extended window for accumulated reproductive experience to enhance offspring survival at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. Ultimately, the unique suite of traits, including a gestation of 34 days [tg = 34 days] and a reproductive rate anchored by 3.29 pups [N_R_i = 3.29 pups] per litter and 2.6 litters per year [F_R_i = 2.6 litters per year], all functioning at a core temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], positions the rakali as a textbook example of a K-selected specialist in an otherwise r-selected mammalian lineage.
